input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Describe construction of the document section graph, node and edge semantics (section dependencies, prerequisite relations), graph serialization, and the leaf-first scheduling algorithm used to order section generation.

output:
We represent a target manuscript as an explicit, machine-readable section graph that captures intended section units and the prerequisite relations among them. The graph is a directed graph G = (V, E) whose nodes V correspond to section-level writing targets (for example, Background, Methods, Experiment A, Discussion) and whose directed edges E encode prerequisite or dependency relations between sections. We treat the graph and the scheduler as design-time artifacts of the generation pipeline: their structure determines the order in which sections are generated, the evidence that is propagated between sections, and the validation checks applied during assembly.

Node semantics. Each node in V is a structured object that at minimum contains (i) a stable identifier, (ii) a human-readable title, (iii) a section role or type (e.g., background, method, result, limitation), (iv) a specification of evidence requirements (e.g., required citation anchors or mandatory data references), and (v) a pointer to the prompt/template to be used for generation. The complete JSON schema for section outputs and node fields is specified in Section 3.2; here we summarize the important design choices. Encoding section-level metadata explicitly (rather than relying solely on a monolithic prompt) makes it possible to: (a) validate that required evidence fields are present prior to assembly, (b) track which sections supply evidence that others may cite, and (c) support iterative edits at the node granularity.

Edge semantics. A directed edge (u → v) indicates that node u is a prerequisite for node v: content and evidence produced for u should be available to the generation of v, and v may rely on claims or citations originating from u. We distinguish several semantic subclasses of edges in practice (captured in an edge-type attribute): evidence-provision (u provides evidence anchors used by v), rhetorical-support (u establishes background claims that v assumes), and refinement (v refines or extends claims first stated in u). Treating edge types as explicit attributes enables the scheduler and evidence-injection protocol to make different tradeoffs (for example, stronger guarantees for evidence-provision edges).

Graph serialization and interoperability. The section graph is serialized as a compact JSON object with top-level arrays for nodes and edges and per-node fields that reference prompt templates and evidence selectors. This serialization is intentionally compatible with the JSON schema described in Section 3.2 so that generated section outputs can be validated and later re-imported for editing or re-generation. Using a standardized serialization facilitates logging, human inspection, and automated checks (for example, verifying that every edge's referenced node id exists and that required evidence fields are satisfied before assembly).

Scheduling algorithm (leaf-first as reverse-dependency ordering). We operationalize ``leaf-first'' scheduling as an explicit dependency-respecting ordering obtained by repeated selection of nodes whose prerequisites are already satisfied. Concretely, the scheduler traverses the directed graph in a reverse-topological fashion: it maintains the set of nodes whose incoming prerequisites are either absent or already generated, selects one (or a small batch) from this set for generation, and after a node is produced marks its outgoing dependents as having one fewer unmet prerequisite. This process continues until all nodes are generated or until no progress can be made (see cycle handling below). The practical effect is that generation proceeds from nodes that do not depend on others toward nodes that aggregate and synthesize earlier outputs, ensuring that dependent sections can cite or explicitly reference evidence produced by their prerequisites.

Batching, parallelism, and pragmatics. The scheduler supports batching and limited parallel generation: when multiple nodes become eligible (no unmet prerequisites), the system may generate them in parallel subject to resource constraints and to policies that prioritize evidence-rich nodes first. Batch sizes and parallelism policies are configurable; the serialized graph and node metadata encode preferred policies where appropriate. Because evidence injection is performed at the node level (see Section 3.3), parallel generation is only allowed when there are no mutual dependencies or shared exclusive evidence locks.

Cycle detection and remediation. Directed cycles indicate mutually dependent sections (for example, two sections that must cite each other's claims). The scheduler includes a cycle-detection step (strongly connected components). When a nontrivial cycle is found the system flags the cycle and offers two conservative remediation strategies: (1) require human annotation to break or reprioritize the dependencies, or (2) convert one or more edges into soft dependencies that permit generation with placeholder anchors that must be resolved in a subsequent refinement pass. The chosen remediation policy is recorded in the graph metadata so that downstream assembly and validation can detect any unresolved placeholders.

Light-weight provenance and change management. Each generated node carries provenance metadata linking the section output to the evidence items used at generation time and to the exact prompt/template version. The provenance fields are embedded in the serialized node and enable downstream checks (for example, verifying that claims in a parent node cite evidence actually produced by its prerequisites). Because the graph is machine-readable, targeted re-generation (regenerating a single node and replaying dependent nodes) is straightforward: the scheduler can re-run only affected nodes while preserving unaffected outputs.

Failure modes and conservative defaults. The graph-and-scheduler design favors conservative defaults: a node is only considered complete if its required evidence fields are populated and JSON validation (Section 3.2) succeeds. Incomplete evidence, unresolved placeholders, or scheduling deadlocks are surfaced as failures rather than silently producing prose. These conservative behaviors simplify auditing and reduce the risk of unsupported assertions being propagated into aggregated sections; Section 3.5 discusses assembly-level checks and operational failure handling in more detail.

Notes on implementation and extensibility. The representation and scheduler described here are intentionally modular: alternative node types (finer-grained paragraph nodes, or dedicated evidence-source nodes) can be added without changing the core traversal logic, and edge types can be extended to capture additional rhetorical relations. The practical benefits, tradeoffs, and quantitative impact of this scheduling strategy are evaluated in the Experiments and Results sections.
